Prompt, Run, Verify

Analysis walkthrough · Workshop 3: Using LLMs for Data Analysis in Public Health

Heather Mattie, PhD · Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health

September 30, 2026

How to use this file. Every code chunk below is the kind of code an LLM will happily write for you. The text between the chunks is the part the LLM can’t do for you: noticing what is wrong. Run each chunk with the green arrow and read the output before moving on. Click Knit to turn the whole file into a report.

First time? Put this file and nhanes_workshop.csv in the same folder, open the file in RStudio, and run this once in the Console: install.packages(c("tidyverse", "gtsummary", "flextable", "broom", "rmarkdown"))

library(tidyverse)   # data import, wrangling, ggplot2
library(gtsummary)   # Table 1 and regression tables
library(flextable)   # export tables to Word / PowerPoint
library(broom)       # tidy model output

1. Import and first look

Data: 1,000 adults sampled from the public NHANES R package (2009–2012 survey cycles), reshaped to look like a typical study extract. The codebook is in section 4 of the Student Guide.

dat_raw <- read_csv("nhanes_workshop.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(dat_raw)
## Rows: 1,000
## Columns: 10
## $ study_id    <chr> "P0001", "P0002", "P0003", "P0004", "P0005", "P0006", "P00…
## $ age         <dbl> 54, 62, 80, 70, 74, 80, 80, 32, 36, 24, 29, 78, 38, 31, 28…
## $ sex         <chr> "male", "female", "male", "male", "female", "female", "fem…
## $ race        <dbl> 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 5, 3, 1, 5, 1, 4, 4, 1, 4, 4, 1, 1, 3…
## $ education   <chr> "Some College", "High School", "Some College", "College Gr…
## $ bmi         <dbl> 23.8, 27.1, 28.3, 25.9, 26.7, 24.8, 29.7, 23.2, 24.3, 18.1…
## $ sbp         <dbl> 154, 129, NA, 121, 127, 138, 135, 116, 182, 101, 108, 193,…
## $ diabetes    <chr> "Yes", "No", "No", "Yes", "No", "No", "No", "No", "No", "N…
## $ phys_active <chr> "No", "No", "No", "Yes", "Yes", "No", "No", "Yes", "No", "…
## $ ever_smoker <chr> "No", "No", "Yes", "No", "No", "No", "Yes", "No", "No", "Y…

Checkpoint (check 2: right dimensions and types?). 1,000 rows, 10 columns — good. But race is stored as a number (dbl). It is a category coded 1–5. R does not know that, and neither will the LLM unless you tell it.

summary(dat_raw)

Checkpoint (check 3: plausible values?). Mean BMI is about 37.6. That alone might not set off alarms — but the maximum is 999. That’s a missing-value code, not a person. The mean was quietly inflated by 9 fake values.

dat_raw |> count(bmi == 999)
## # A tibble: 2 × 2
##   `bmi == 999`     n
##   <lgl>        <int>
## 1 FALSE          991
## 2 TRUE             9

2. Clean — the step that needs you

These decisions come from the codebook and your domain knowledge, not from the LLM.

dat <- dat_raw |>
  mutate(
    bmi  = na_if(bmi, 999),                       # 999 = missing (codebook)
    race = factor(race, levels = 1:5,
                  labels = c("White", "Black", "Mexican American",
                             "Other Hispanic", "Other/Multiracial")),
    sex  = factor(sex, levels = c("female", "male"),
                  labels = c("Female", "Male")),
    education = factor(education,
                       levels = c("8th Grade", "9 - 11th Grade", "High School",
                                  "Some College", "College Grad")),
    diabetes    = factor(diabetes,    levels = c("No", "Yes")),
    phys_active = factor(phys_active, levels = c("No", "Yes")),
    ever_smoker = factor(ever_smoker, levels = c("No", "Yes"))
  )

summary(dat$bmi)   # now plausible: max 62.8, 9 NA
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
##   15.80   24.20   28.10   28.88   32.45   62.80       9

3. Descriptive statistics

dat |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  summarize(n        = n(),
            mean_age = mean(age),
            mean_bmi = mean(bmi, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_sbp = mean(sbp, na.rm = TRUE),
            n_missing_sbp = sum(is.na(sbp)))
## # A tibble: 2 × 6
##   sex        n mean_age mean_bmi mean_sbp n_missing_sbp
##   <fct>  <int>    <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>         <int>
## 1 Female   511     48.8     29.1     119.            24
## 2 Male     489     45.8     28.6     123.            17

Checkpoint. Do the group sizes add to 1,000? Are missing values counted, not silently dropped?

4. Visualizations

ggplot(dat, aes(x = bmi)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = crimson, color = "white") +
  labs(x = "BMI (kg/m2)", y = "Number of participants",
       title = "Distribution of BMI") +
  theme_minimal()
## Warning: Removed 9 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
## (`stat_bin()`).

ggplot(dat, aes(x = bmi, y = sbp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, color = "#5F5256") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = crimson, fill = "#E8D3D7") +
  facet_wrap(~ sex) +
  labs(x = "BMI (kg/m2)", y = "Systolic blood pressure (mmHg)",
       title = "BMI and systolic blood pressure, by sex") +
  theme_minimal()
## Warning: Removed 48 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
## (`stat_smooth()`).
## Warning: Removed 48 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).

Notice the warning about removed rows: R is telling you some rows had missing BMI or SBP. Read warnings; don’t scroll past them.

dat |>
  count(phys_active, diabetes) |>
  group_by(phys_active) |>
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) |>
  filter(diabetes == "Yes") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = phys_active, y = pct)) +
  geom_col(fill = crimson, width = 0.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Physically active", y = "Diabetes prevalence",
       title = "Diabetes prevalence by physical activity") +
  theme_minimal()

5. Table 1

table1 <- dat |>
  select(age, sex, race, education, bmi, sbp, phys_active, ever_smoker, diabetes) |>
  tbl_summary(
    by = diabetes,
    label = list(age ~ "Age (years)", sex ~ "Sex", race ~ "Race/ethnicity",
                 education ~ "Education", bmi ~ "BMI (kg/m2)",
                 sbp ~ "Systolic BP (mmHg)", phys_active ~ "Physically active",
                 ever_smoker ~ "Smoked 100+ cigarettes"),
    statistic = list(all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})"),
    missing_text = "Missing"
  ) |>
  add_overall() |>
  modify_spanning_header(c("stat_1", "stat_2") ~ "**Diabetes**") |>
  bold_labels()

Checkpoint (domain check). Should Table 1 include p-values? Many journals and methodologists (e.g., CONSORT for trials) say no. The LLM will add them if you ask, and often if you don’t. That’s a judgment call, not a coding question.

6. Regression models

Linear regression: systolic BP

fit_lm <- lm(sbp ~ bmi + age + sex + race, data = dat)

tbl_regression(fit_lm,
               label = list(bmi ~ "BMI (per 1 kg/m2)", age ~ "Age (per year)",
                            sex ~ "Sex", race ~ "Race/ethnicity")) |>
  add_glance_source_note(include = c(nobs, r.squared)) |>
  as_flex_table()

Checkpoint (check 2 again). Table 1 has 1,000 people. How many are in the model?

nobs(fit_lm)
## [1] 952

Rows with missing BMI or SBP were dropped (complete-case analysis). That should be reported in your methods, and it is a choice worth discussing with your advisor.

Logistic regression: diabetes

fit_glm <- glm(diabetes ~ bmi + age + sex + phys_active,
               data = dat, family = binomial)

tbl_regression(fit_glm, exponentiate = TRUE,
               label = list(bmi ~ "BMI (per 1 kg/m2)", age ~ "Age (per year)",
                            sex ~ "Sex", phys_active ~ "Physically active")) |>
  as_flex_table()

Checkpoint (interpretation). These are odds ratios, not risk ratios. With about 9% prevalence the two are close here, but the gap grows as an outcome gets more common, and an LLM summary rarely checks. The data are cross-sectional: associations, not effects. LLM summaries often blur both.

7. Check 4: test on a tiny example with a known answer

test <- tibble(
  sex = c("F", "F", "F", "M", "M", "M"),
  sbp = c(120, 130, NA, 140, 150, 160)
)
# Expected by hand: F = 125, M = 150
test |> group_by(sex) |> summarize(mean_sbp = mean(sbp, na.rm = TRUE))
## # A tibble: 2 × 2
##   sex   mean_sbp
##   <chr>    <dbl>
## 1 F          125
## 2 M          150

If this returned 83.3 for F, the code would be treating NA as 0. You found the bug on 6 rows instead of in your manuscript.

8. Text vs. numbers demo

These are the 25 values from the “Try it” exercise. Paste them into a chat with code execution turned off and ask for the mean and standard deviation. Then compare with what R computes below.

set.seed(27)
bp25 <- dat |> filter(!is.na(sbp)) |> slice_sample(n = 25) |> pull(sbp)
cat(bp25, sep = ", ")
## 130, 118, 100, 119, 96, 90, 120, 148, 114, 130, 99, 124, 131, 130, 148, 98, 118, 114, 113, 134, 116, 143, 158, 112, 110
c(mean = mean(bp25), sd = sd(bp25))
##      mean        sd 
## 120.52000  17.41436

The model predicts digits that look like a mean. Code computes one.

9. The no-upload path (restricted data)

When data can’t leave approved systems, give the LLM the structure, not the data. Example prompt:

Context: I’m working in R with the tidyverse and gtsummary. My data frame dat has 1,000 rows. Columns: age (numeric, 20–80), sex (character: “female”/“male”, lowercase), race (integer 1–5; 1=White, 2=Black, 3=Mexican American, 4=Other Hispanic, 5=Other/Multiracial), bmi (numeric; 999 = missing), sbp (numeric, some NA), diabetes (“No”/“Yes”). Objective: Create a Table 1 comparing participants with and without diabetes, and fit a linear regression of sbp on bmi, age, sex, and race. Format: One commented R code chunk. First, write code that creates a fake 50-row data frame with this exact structure so I can test the code without real data.

Below is the kind of fake-data code the LLM returns. You develop against it, then run the finished code on the real data inside the approved environment.

set.seed(1)
fake <- tibble(
  age      = sample(20:80, 50, replace = TRUE),
  sex      = sample(c("female", "male"), 50, replace = TRUE),
  race     = sample(1:5, 50, replace = TRUE),
  bmi      = c(round(rnorm(48, 28, 6), 1), 999, 999),
  sbp      = c(round(rnorm(48, 120, 15)), NA, NA),
  diabetes = sample(c("No", "Yes"), 50, replace = TRUE, prob = c(.9, .1))
)
glimpse(fake)
## Rows: 50
## Columns: 6
## $ age      <int> 76, 23, 58, 20, 53, 80, 42, 62, 33, 37, 78, 70, 52, 40, 40, 6…
## $ sex      <chr> "female", "male", "male", "female", "female", "male", "male",…
## $ race     <int> 4, 1, 5, 5, 1, 1, 3, 2, 2, 3, 2, 4, 3, 5, 2, 2, 1, 3, 3, 2, 2…
## $ bmi      <dbl> 24.7, 35.2, 35.0, 32.2, 37.5, 31.4, 20.3, 24.6, 20.7, 25.2, 2…
## $ sbp      <dbl> 110, 119, 91, 138, 95, 113, 103, 109, 151, 120, 101, 95, 127,…
## $ diabetes <chr> "Yes", "No", "No", "No", "No", "No", "No", "No", "No", "No", …

Note what made this work: the prompt said “lowercase,” “999 = missing,” and “integer 1–5.” Leave those out and the code will run and be wrong (see Spot the bug in section 5 of the Student Guide).

10. Exporting results

Same source, many outputs:

dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)

# Table 1 -> Word and PowerPoint
table1 |> as_flex_table() |> save_as_docx(path = "output/table1.docx")
table1 |> as_flex_table() |> save_as_pptx(path = "output/table1.pptx")

# Regression table -> Word
tbl_regression(fit_lm) |> as_flex_table() |>
  save_as_docx(path = "output/regression_sbp.docx")

# Figure -> PNG (for slides) and PDF (for journals)
p <- ggplot(dat, aes(bmi, sbp)) + geom_point(alpha = .35, color = "#5F5256") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = crimson, fill = "#E8D3D7") + theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "BMI (kg/m2)", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)")
ggsave("output/bmi_sbp.png", p, width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 300)
## Warning: Removed 48 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
## (`stat_smooth()`).
## Warning: Removed 48 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).
ggsave("output/bmi_sbp.pdf", p, width = 6, height = 4)
## Warning: Removed 48 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
## (`stat_smooth()`).
## Removed 48 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).
# Clean data -> CSV
write_csv(dat, "output/nhanes_clean.csv")

list.files("output")
## [1] "bmi_sbp.pdf"         "bmi_sbp.png"         "nhanes_clean.csv"   
## [4] "regression_sbp.docx" "table1.docx"         "table1.pptx"

Why this beats downloading a .docx from the chat window: this file reruns from raw data to final tables. When a reviewer asks you to drop 20 participants, you change one line and knit again.
